source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6

coverage.syllabusAssignment: Chapter 6, pp. 355–415: Exemptions, Guidance & Agency Choice
coverage.status: Required rulemaking, petitions and waiver doctrine and cases. Textbook hypotheticals unsolved.

topics.title: § 6.2 — Required Rulemaking, Bell Aerospace & State Variations (pp. 389–397)
topics.description: Chenery II discretionary choice, Bell Aerospace, reliance consequences, state required rulemaking and Madison student-parking discipline problem.

entries.title: Default federal agency freedom to make policy in rulemaking or adjudication
entries.summary: Unless controlling law dictates otherwise, an agency generally may make law by rule or by precedent established in an individual proceeding; judges rarely force notice-and-comment before a new general policy.
entries.laymanExplanation: Unless controlling law dictates otherwise, an agency generally may make law by rule or by precedent established in an individual proceeding; judges rarely force notice-and-comment before a new general policy.
entries.legalExplanation: An agency can announce a new policy while deciding a case, rather than always first writing a regulation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 389–393
entries.examApplication: Chenery II and Bell Aerospace stress agency's informed discretion; hard facts may be better handled incrementally.
entries.examTrap: Don't claim all rulelike policy statements made in adjudication automatically violate § 553.

entries.title: NLRB v. Bell Aerospace Co., 416 U.S. 267 (1974)
entries.summary: No. NLRB may develop legal doctrine through case-by-case adjudication; Court of Appeals could not require rulemaking here.
entries.laymanExplanation: No. NLRB may develop legal doctrine through case-by-case adjudication; Court of Appeals could not require rulemaking here.
entries.legalExplanation: Case application: Must NLRB conduct notice-and-comment rulemaking rather than adjudication to reconsider whether particular employees qualify as managerial under NLRA? Chenery II and Wyman-Gordon recognize discretion to develop standards through orders. Buyers' duties vary vastly across businesses, making universal rule hard. Parties in concrete case can contribute facts. Agency reliance concerns did not reach level warranting exceptional intervention—no fines, retroactive new liability or shown severe reliance losses.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 390–393
entries.facts: United Auto Workers sought election to represent buyers employed at Bell Aerospace facility; company argued they were 'managerial employees' excluded from NLRA. Board's interpretation appeared to change longstanding policy; Second Circuit ordered NLRB to adopt new approach only by rulemaking. Supreme Court agreed with lower court on substantive managerial-employee issue but rejected mandated rulemaking approach.
entries.issue: Must NLRB conduct notice-and-comment rulemaking rather than adjudication to reconsider whether particular employees qualify as managerial under NLRA?
entries.holding: No. NLRB may develop legal doctrine through case-by-case adjudication; Court of Appeals could not require rulemaking here.
entries.reasoning: Chenery II and Wyman-Gordon recognize discretion to develop standards through orders. Buyers' duties vary vastly across businesses, making universal rule hard. Parties in concrete case can contribute facts. Agency reliance concerns did not reach level warranting exceptional intervention—no fines, retroactive new liability or shown severe reliance losses.
entries.rule: The choice between rulemaking and adjudication lies primarily with the agency's informed discretion; potentially limited by abuse of discretion, statute or unusually serious retroactive unfairness.
entries.exam: Compare first-case policymaking to a binding policy statement; discuss reason for varying facts and unsettled future employment classifications.
entries.examTrap: Bell Aerospace does not hold agencies can retroactively punish fair-reliant parties without limit.

entries.title: SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery II), 332 U.S. 194 (1947)
entries.summary: Agency may formulate new standard in adjudication, especially with unanticipated, fact-specific, evolving issues, rather than mandatory general rule.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency may formulate new standard in adjudication, especially with unanticipated, fact-specific, evolving issues, rather than mandatory general rule.
entries.legalExplanation: Chenery II quotations supply primary basis for Bell Aerospace.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 391–392
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not excerpted

entries.title: NLRB v. Wyman-Gordon Co., 394 U.S. 759 (1969)
entries.summary: Adjudicated decisions may announce generally influential policy and provide future guidance.
entries.laymanExplanation: Adjudicated decisions may announce generally influential policy and provide future guidance.
entries.legalExplanation: Further supports agency's discretion to choose cases as policymaking vehicles.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 392
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Adjudicative precedent cannot always become unrebuttable rule
entries.summary: When agency uses case law to develop policy, later litigants should retain meaningful ability to distinguish or contest the precedent on relevant facts; blanket refusal can be arbitrary.
entries.laymanExplanation: When agency uses case law to develop policy, later litigants should retain meaningful ability to distinguish or contest the precedent on relevant facts; blanket refusal can be arbitrary.
entries.legalExplanation: Earlier NLRB case is precedent, but it does not bar hearings on genuinely different factual context if governing law requires case-specific evaluation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 393–394
entries.examApplication: Distinguish Bell Aerospace's open consideration of relevant information from St. Francis Hospital's refusal to take evidence.

entries.title: NLRB v. St. Francis Hospital, 601 F.2d 404 (9th Cir. 1979)
entries.summary: NLRB improperly treated earlier nurse unit precedent as conclusive and refused relevant factual evidence about alternative unit.
entries.laymanExplanation: NLRB improperly treated earlier nurse unit precedent as conclusive and refused relevant factual evidence about alternative unit.
entries.legalExplanation: Court considered refusal arbitrary and capricious; different from merely choosing adjudication.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 393–394
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Reliance and limits on retroactive adjudicative policymaking
entries.summary: Severe harm to persons who trusted old agency precedent, retroactive new liability or fines/damages can make adjudicative application unreasonable or violate fair notice.
entries.laymanExplanation: Severe harm to persons who trusted old agency precedent, retroactive new liability or fines/damages can make adjudicative application unreasonable or violate fair notice.
entries.legalExplanation: Preferred remedy often protect particular regulated party from unfair retroactive penalty, not force agency to make new rule.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 394
entries.examApplication: Use Retail, Wholesale balancing, Fox II, and facts on fair notice, justified reliance and statutory interest.
entries.examTrap: The new precedent may remain valid prospectively even if unfairly applied to earlier behavior.

entries.title: State law may compel rulemaking before broad prospective policy
entries.summary: Some states, unlike ordinary federal practice, require agencies to elaborate vague standards by rule or treat general policies used in adjudication as de facto rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some states, unlike ordinary federal practice, require agencies to elaborate vague standards by rule or treat general policies used in adjudication as de facto rules.
entries.legalExplanation: Always ask jurisdiction and state APA wording rather than reflexively relying on federal Bell Aerospace.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 394–396

entries.title: Megdal v. Oregon Board of Dental Examiners, 605 P.2d 273 (Or. 1980)
entries.summary: Oregon court reversed dentist license sanction under undefined 'unprofessional conduct' without prior clarifying standards; inferred legislative intent toward rulemaking.
entries.laymanExplanation: Oregon court reversed dentist license sanction under undefined 'unprofessional conduct' without prior clarifying standards; inferred legislative intent toward rulemaking.
entries.legalExplanation: Later Oregon decisions resisted across-the-board rulemaking presumption, instead analyze multiple statutory indicia.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 394–395
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Oregon's later restrained approach to Megdal
entries.summary: Current casebook description notes later Oregon cases decide required-rulemaking issues through contextual legislature-intent inquiry, not a blanket rule that every broad standard needs rule.
entries.laymanExplanation: Current casebook description notes later Oregon cases decide required-rulemaking issues through contextual legislature-intent inquiry, not a blanket rule that every broad standard needs rule.
entries.legalExplanation: Do not exaggerate Megdal into universally binding broad Oregon rule.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 395
entries.examApplication: Examine whether similar professional licensing statutes express procedural expectations.

entries.title: Florida: feasible and practicable general policy requires rulemaking
entries.summary: Florida § 120.54(1)(a) presumptively requires rulemaking for generally applicable future policy when feasible and practicable; burden on agency to show otherwise.
entries.laymanExplanation: Florida § 120.54(1)(a) presumptively requires rulemaking for generally applicable future policy when feasible and practicable; burden on agency to show otherwise.
entries.legalExplanation: Florida flips federal default: if policy can practically be articulated as a general rule, agencies should use rulemaking.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 395–396
entries.examApplication: Consider companion statutory restrictions on scope of agency rule power and waiver obligations.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume this means agencies may issue a rule without specific enabling statutory power.

entries.title: State due process and advance standards cases
entries.summary: Older state and federal decisions sometimes insisted on published standards before severe individual deprivations under open-ended statutory terms.
entries.laymanExplanation: Older state and federal decisions sometimes insisted on published standards before severe individual deprivations under open-ended statutory terms.
entries.legalExplanation: Historical cases included welfare, discipline and professional licensing; book raises whether to revive as broader rule.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 395

entries.title: Florida's 1996 APA tradeoffs
entries.summary: Florida retained presumption for rulemaking but imposed narrower specific statutory delegation, wider waivers, heightened analysis and greater agency burdens in rule challenges.
entries.laymanExplanation: Florida retained presumption for rulemaking but imposed narrower specific statutory delegation, wider waivers, heightened analysis and greater agency burdens in rule challenges.
entries.legalExplanation: Procedural rigor can coexist with limits on agency power and flexibility from exceptions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 396

topics.title: § 6.3 — Petitions, Agency Priorities & Massachusetts v. EPA (pp. 397–406)
topics.description: APA petition rights and denial, statutory constraints on EPA, extreme deference, deadlines, delay and horse-soring hypothetical.

entries.title: Rulemaking petitions under APA § 553(e)
entries.summary: Interested persons may petition for issuance, amendment or repeal of rule; petition provides way to request policy change or contest rules issued without prior public input.
entries.laymanExplanation: Interested persons may petition for issuance, amendment or repeal of rule; petition provides way to request policy change or contest rules issued without prior public input.
entries.legalExplanation: You can ask agency to start, change or undo a rule even if not present in original comment period.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 397
entries.examApplication: Federal APA § 555(e) requires brief statement of grounds for denial; petition right does not guarantee grant.

entries.title: Model state petition deadline versus federal no deadline
entries.summary: 1961 MSAPA § 6 requires denial with reasons or initiation of rulemaking within 30 days; federal APA has no matching fixed petition-response clock.
entries.laymanExplanation: 1961 MSAPA § 6 requires denial with reasons or initiation of rulemaking within 30 days; federal APA has no matching fixed petition-response clock.
entries.legalExplanation: A federal petition may linger, triggering separate unreasonable-delay questions; state model expressly requires quick agency reply.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 397–398, 403

entries.title: Judicial review of petition denial exists but is highly deferential
entries.summary: Refusal to start rulemaking ordinarily is reviewable, but receives especially deferential arbitrary-and-capricious review given agency priority setting; distinguish largely unreviewable nonenforcement decisions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Refusal to start rulemaking ordinarily is reviewable, but receives especially deferential arbitrary-and-capricious review given agency priority setting; distinguish largely unreviewable nonenforcement decisions.
entries.legalExplanation: Agency cannot ignore law, but judges usually don't rearrange agency's budget and priorities.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 398–402
entries.examApplication: Analyze whether agency misconstrued its jurisdiction, rested decision on improper statutory factors, or ignored dispositive evidence.
entries.examTrap: Do not confuse § 553(e) petition denial with Heckler v. Chaney nonenforcement presumption.

entries.title: Massachusetts v. EPA, 549 U.S. 497 (2007)
entries.summary: No. Supreme Court found CO2 and other greenhouse gases within Act's pollutant definition and EPA's reasons for refusing to make statutory endangerment judgment inadequate. EPA decision arbitrary and capricious; remand required lawful statutory reasoning, not immediate compelled endangerment finding.
entries.laymanExplanation: No. Supreme Court found CO2 and other greenhouse gases within Act's pollutant definition and EPA's reasons for refusing to make statutory endangerment judgment inadequate. EPA decision arbitrary and capricious; remand required lawful statutory reasoning, not immediate compelled endangerment finding.
entries.legalExplanation: Case application: Could EPA refuse to address greenhouse-gas endangerment petition based on mistaken reading of 'air pollutant' and policy considerations outside statutory endangerment inquiry? Discretion is broad but bounded by statutory directions. Congress required EPA to exercise scientific judgment concerning endangerment. EPA could decline to move forward if gases did not contribute or if genuinely unable to make reasoned scientific judgment, not because President preferred voluntary measures or foreign diplomatic programs.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 398–401
entries.facts: Massachusetts and others petitioned EPA for rules controlling greenhouse-gas emissions from new motor vehicles under Clean Air Act § 202(a)(1). EPA said greenhouse gases not covered 'air pollutants' and alternatively cited scientific uncertainty, voluntary executive programs, foreign policy and preference for broad nonregulatory approach. Court's 5–4 majority had earlier found standing.
entries.issue: Could EPA refuse to address greenhouse-gas endangerment petition based on mistaken reading of 'air pollutant' and policy considerations outside statutory endangerment inquiry?
entries.holding: No. Supreme Court found CO2 and other greenhouse gases within Act's pollutant definition and EPA's reasons for refusing to make statutory endangerment judgment inadequate. EPA decision arbitrary and capricious; remand required lawful statutory reasoning, not immediate compelled endangerment finding.
entries.reasoning: Discretion is broad but bounded by statutory directions. Congress required EPA to exercise scientific judgment concerning endangerment. EPA could decline to move forward if gases did not contribute or if genuinely unable to make reasoned scientific judgment, not because President preferred voluntary measures or foreign diplomatic programs.
entries.rule: Once agency responds to petition, reasons for acting or not acting must be grounded in enabling statute; review exceptionally deferential but legal error and irrelevant statutory rationale invalid.
entries.exam: Separate majority's statutory merits from standing, whether greenhouse-gas endangerment found on remand, and remedial scope. Include Scalia dissent's broader view of power to defer forming judgment.
entries.examTrap: Book excerpts historical 2007 decision; do not infer present EPA climate rule status from this chapter alone.

entries.title: Massachusetts v EPA: Scalia dissent's priorities argument
entries.summary: Four dissenters read CAA discretion to decide when to make scientific judgment as allowing broader policy and resource considerations, absent text dictating timing.
entries.laymanExplanation: Four dissenters read CAA discretion to decide when to make scientific judgment as allowing broader policy and resource considerations, absent text dictating timing.
entries.legalExplanation: Majority constrained EPA to statutory endangerment-focused reasons; dissent would uphold refusal to form judgment now.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 400–401
entries.examApplication: On exam contrast which statutory text governs permissible rationale, not merely judge's environmental preferences.

entries.title: Defenders of Wildlife v. Gutierrez, 532 F.3d 913 (D.C. Cir. 2008)
entries.summary: Agency reasonably prioritized comprehensive whale-ship-collision regulation instead of emergency speed rule; petition denial upheld even after extended delay.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency reasonably prioritized comprehensive whale-ship-collision regulation instead of emergency speed rule; petition denial upheld even after extended delay.
entries.legalExplanation: Demonstrates very high deference to scientifically focused agency priorities.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 401–402
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not excerpted

entries.title: NAACP v. FPC, 520 F.2d 432 (D.C. Cir. 1975)
entries.summary: Agency refusal based on wrong view of regulatory jurisdiction set aside; remand for reconsideration, not compulsory ultimate rule.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency refusal based on wrong view of regulatory jurisdiction set aside; remand for reconsideration, not compulsory ultimate rule.
entries.legalExplanation: Shows legal-error exception to deferential refusal review.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 402–403
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Rios v. Department of Labor & Industries, 39 P.3d 961 (Wash. 2002)
entries.summary: Washington court rejected workforce-safety agency's refusal to adopt pesticide blood-testing rule after expert committee found program feasible and necessary; agency cited competing resources.
entries.laymanExplanation: Washington court rejected workforce-safety agency's refusal to adopt pesticide blood-testing rule after expert committee found program feasible and necessary; agency cited competing resources.
entries.legalExplanation: Illustrates more searching state review and tension between expert evidence and priority-setting freedom.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 403
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Delays and mandatory rulemaking deadlines
entries.summary: Congress sometimes imposes fixed rule deadlines; courts differ on remedies and whether literal statutory command compels agency despite scarce resources.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress sometimes imposes fixed rule deadlines; courts differ on remedies and whether literal statutory command compels agency despite scarce resources.
entries.legalExplanation: A missed deadline does not always yield same judicial action; assess law, remedy, competing agency obligations.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 403–405
entries.examApplication: Forest Guardians enforced 'shall'; In re Barr Laboratories favored resource triage.

entries.title: APA § 706(1): agency action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed
entries.summary: Reviewing courts can compel legally required agency action in circumstances of unlawful withholding or unreasonable delay; discretionary remedy weighs time, statutory context, harm and resources.
entries.laymanExplanation: Reviewing courts can compel legally required agency action in circumstances of unlawful withholding or unreasonable delay; discretionary remedy weighs time, statutory context, harm and resources.
entries.legalExplanation: Petitioner may demand agency finally act on a long-delayed rulemaking, but judge must consider complexity and competing safety priorities.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 404–405
entries.examApplication: Distinguish deadline violation, indefinite delay and decision whether to regulate at all.

entries.title: In re International Chemical Workers Union, 958 F.2d 1144 (D.C. Cir. 1992)
entries.summary: OSHA's six-year delay on cadmium standard was unreasonable; court ordered prompt final action, weighing known health risks and broken agency deadlines.
entries.laymanExplanation: OSHA's six-year delay on cadmium standard was unreasonable; court ordered prompt final action, weighing known health risks and broken agency deadlines.
entries.legalExplanation: Book lists four factors: duration since duty arose; statutory context; consequences; administrative error, difficulty and priorities.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 404
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not excerpted

entries.title: State lapse rules and periodic retrospective review
entries.summary: Some states void uncompleted rulemaking after statutory period; federal APA lacks general lapse deadline. Regulatory Flexibility Act § 610 requires ten-year review of certain small-entity-impact rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some states void uncompleted rulemaking after statutory period; federal APA lacks general lapse deadline. Regulatory Flexibility Act § 610 requires ten-year review of certain small-entity-impact rules.
entries.legalExplanation: Retroactive review can discover obsolete regulation, but mandatory review itself consumes capacity; voluntary reviews may result in more changes.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 404–405
entries.examApplication: Do not mistake presidential review programs mentioned in text as necessarily current executive orders.

entries.title: The agency agenda-setting tension
entries.summary: Petitions democratize agenda and offer alternatives to stale policy; agency has resource limits, expertise and evolving industries; courts reconcile statute with efficiency.
entries.laymanExplanation: Petitions democratize agenda and offer alternatives to stale policy; agency has resource limits, expertise and evolving industries; courts reconcile statute with efficiency.
entries.legalExplanation: A well-supported petition deserves explanation but cannot always displace agency's strongest existing work.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 397–405

topics.title: § 6.4 — Waivers, WAIT Radio & Regulatory Exceptions (pp. 406–415)
topics.description: Waiver safety-valve, meaningful agency consideration, abuse of discretion, mandatory Florida variances, structured and big waiver, FHWA monocular-driver problem.

entries.title: Waiver or variance of regulation
entries.summary: Agency authorized to excuse particular regulated person from otherwise applicable generally valid rule because of special facts consistent with statutory and policy objectives.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency authorized to excuse particular regulated person from otherwise applicable generally valid rule because of special facts consistent with statutory and policy objectives.
entries.legalExplanation: A lawful exception can avoid unjust result without destroying general rule.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 406–407

entries.title: Waivers as safety valve for general standards
entries.summary: Legitimate agency regulation by generalized rule may require room for meritorious unusual circumstances; waiver may serve statutory public interest better in individual facts.
entries.laymanExplanation: Legitimate agency regulation by generalized rule may require room for meritorious unusual circumstances; waiver may serve statutory public interest better in individual facts.
entries.legalExplanation: The general rule stays valid; special applicant asks to be treated differently without undermining it.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 407–409
entries.examApplication: Ask exact hardship/special facts, conflict with rule purposes, agency authority, consistent decision standards and effects on third parties.
entries.examTrap: An application for waiver normally assumes applicant otherwise violates the rule.

entries.title: WAIT Radio v. FCC, 418 F.2d 1153 (D.C. Cir. 1969)
entries.summary: FCC rejection insufficiently explained; D.C. Circuit remanded for reasoned evaluation rather than granting waiver itself.
entries.laymanExplanation: FCC rejection insufficiently explained; D.C. Circuit remanded for reasoned evaluation rather than granting waiver itself.
entries.legalExplanation: Case application: Must FCC genuinely consider specific evidence that waiver serves public interest and core rule goals, or may it summarily reject waiver because applicant would otherwise violate general regulation? General rule presumption strong and applicants must plead special facts with documentary support. But agency cannot treat violation of rule as dispositive against waiver, which is the point of exception. Serious, fact-backed allegations require a 'hard look' and intelligible explanation; waivers under principled standards preserve administrative flexibility.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 406–409
entries.facts: FCC clear-channel limits allowed WAIT Chicago AM station at 820 kHz to broadcast only in daylight to avoid nighttime interference with protected distant radio service. WAIT requested nighttime waiver, planned directional antenna avoiding interference with Texas stations, and claimed distinctive Chicago music/public-affairs programming. FCC rejected without meaningfully assessing evidence and seemed to view deviation from rule as reason itself to deny.
entries.issue: Must FCC genuinely consider specific evidence that waiver serves public interest and core rule goals, or may it summarily reject waiver because applicant would otherwise violate general regulation?
entries.holding: FCC rejection insufficiently explained; D.C. Circuit remanded for reasoned evaluation rather than granting waiver itself.
entries.reasoning: General rule presumption strong and applicants must plead special facts with documentary support. But agency cannot treat violation of rule as dispositive against waiver, which is the point of exception. Serious, fact-backed allegations require a 'hard look' and intelligible explanation; waivers under principled standards preserve administrative flexibility.
entries.rule: Proper supported waiver petition warrants genuine individualized consideration and discernible reasons; agency retains discretion to deny on rational grounds consistent with rule purposes.
entries.exam: Identify clear-channel interference rationale, antenna plan, distinct programming and thin agency reasoning; distinguish remand from award.
entries.examTrap: Do not say every waiver must be granted or every generalized plea warrants extensive opinion; subsequent fuller FCC denial was affirmed.

entries.title: Waiver applicant's prima facie burden
entries.summary: Petitioner must identify particular facts and circumstances that justify departure; generalized pleas do not force exhaustive agency review.
entries.laymanExplanation: Petitioner must identify particular facts and circumstances that justify departure; generalized pleas do not force exhaustive agency review.
entries.legalExplanation: Specific documented exemption case raises stronger obligation to consider; normal rule application receives special presumption of regularity.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 407–409, 415
entries.examApplication: Mention footnote: not every application needs essay; reviewing court should discern agency's 'why and wherefore'.

entries.title: Courts require clear reasons but defer on waiver merits
entries.summary: Waivers can be highly discretionary; appellate court checks abuse of discretion rather than replacing agency's preferred policy with its own.
entries.laymanExplanation: Waivers can be highly discretionary; appellate court checks abuse of discretion rather than replacing agency's preferred policy with its own.
entries.legalExplanation: Court can remand vague decision for explanation, not automatically substitute compassion for legal standards.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 407–412
entries.examApplication: Distinguish defective explanation, evidentiary disregard and rational policy choice.

entries.title: Limits: some valid rules admit no waivers
entries.summary: Certainty, safety and administrative simplicity can justify rigid application even when some applicants face hardship.
entries.laymanExplanation: Certainty, safety and administrative simplicity can justify rigid application even when some applicants face hardship.
entries.legalExplanation: WAIT Radio does not create unconditional constitutional waiver entitlement for every rule.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 410–411
entries.examApplication: Look at agency authority, statutory limits, scientific uncertainty, risks, costs of sorting claimants and uniformity.

entries.title: BellSouth Corp. v. FCC, 162 F.3d 1215 (D.C. Cir. 1999)
entries.summary: Agency can strictly follow general rule where certainty and easy administration reasonably outweigh hardship.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency can strictly follow general rule where certainty and easy administration reasonably outweigh hardship.
entries.legalExplanation: Limits mandatory-waiver reading of WAIT Radio.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 410–411
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Baker v. FAA, 917 F.2d 318 (7th Cir. 1990)
entries.summary: Agency refusal to waive historic pilot age-60 limitation sustained due to aviation safety despite hardship for fit older pilots.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency refusal to waive historic pilot age-60 limitation sustained due to aviation safety despite hardship for fit older pilots.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook notes Congress later raised pilot age limit to 65 in 2007.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 411
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Alizoti v. Gonzales, 477 F.3d 448 (6th Cir. 2007)
entries.summary: Court deferred to BIA's refusal to reconsider immigration motion despite sympathetic marriage-paperwork problem; dissent favored common-sense correction.
entries.laymanExplanation: Court deferred to BIA's refusal to reconsider immigration motion despite sympathetic marriage-paperwork problem; dissent favored common-sense correction.
entries.legalExplanation: Illustrates judicial reluctance to substitute own equities for discretionary waiver choice.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 411–412
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in textbook notes; opinion not excerpted

entries.title: Structured waiver and EPA Project XL
entries.summary: Agencies may deliberately run limited exceptions programs allowing compliant alternatives to one-size-fits-all rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agencies may deliberately run limited exceptions programs allowing compliant alternatives to one-size-fits-all rules.
entries.legalExplanation: Projects aim to enhance innovation, testing and responsiveness, but require guardrails.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 412

entries.title: Waiver process risks: favoritism, opaque exceptions, underenforcement
entries.summary: Without transparent objective standards, waivers can favor privileged actors or erode statutes and equal treatment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Without transparent objective standards, waivers can favor privileged actors or erode statutes and equal treatment.
entries.legalExplanation: Notice, published standards, documented reasons and other-party protections may reduce concerns.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 412
entries.examApplication: Book identifies some state laws that require waiver standards before exemptions may be granted.

entries.title: Florida mandatory variance provision § 120.542
entries.summary: Under textbook's Florida statute summary, waiver required when applicant shows statutory purpose achieved by alternate means plus substantial hardship or violation of fairness.
entries.laymanExplanation: Under textbook's Florida statute summary, waiver required when applicant shows statutory purpose achieved by alternate means plus substantial hardship or violation of fairness.
entries.legalExplanation: Florida makes some waivers mandatory rather than merely discretionary, while retaining core statutory goals.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 412–413
entries.examApplication: Apply each statutory element separately: equivalent statutory compliance and hardship/fairness; don't assume rule can be nullified across board.

entries.title: Big waiver
entries.summary: Statutorily authorized large-scale exception from established federal program requirements for states or major groups, often to permit experimentation and alternative approaches.
entries.laymanExplanation: Statutorily authorized large-scale exception from established federal program requirements for states or major groups, often to permit experimentation and alternative approaches.
entries.legalExplanation: Instead of letting one person deviate from rule, big waiver redesigns delivery of broad education or health program within statutory permissions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, pp. 413–414

entries.title: Big waiver competing theories
entries.summary: Barron/Rakoff favor large-scale flexibility and innovation in rigid social programs; critics Hamburger/McCuskey fear favoritism, opaque executive power and undermining democratic statutory bargain.
entries.laymanExplanation: Barron/Rakoff favor large-scale flexibility and innovation in rigid social programs; critics Hamburger/McCuskey fear favoritism, opaque executive power and undermining democratic statutory bargain.

problems.title: FHWA monocular drivers and Bert waiver problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 6, p. 414–415
problems.prompt: FHWA 1937 rule required 20/40 sight each eye, later pilot experimental exemptions for safe monocular drivers; initial public-safety challenge caused remand, agency reaffirmed safety. Bert with 22 accident-free years missed filing deadline and was refused waiver over precedent concerns. Analyze initial safety showing, Bert decision reasons and alternative Florida waiver statute—do not decide.
